To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bit complexity of solving a zero-dimensional polynomial systems is linear in the input size and that the bit complexity for finding separating linear forms is linear in the number of variables.
the complexity of solving a zero-dimensional system is determined by the complexity of solving one-dimensional systems.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: What is the complexity of solving a zero-dimensional system of polynomials in one variable?
the question of whether the projection approach is a suitable alternative to the well-established methods of Gröbner bases or resultant matrices for solving zero-dimensional systems.

the following question: Given a zero-dimensional integer polynomial system, can one compute all complex solutions and a corresponding linear form with coefficients of small bitsize in time and bit complexity that is essentially linear in the number of variables and the bit complexity of the input?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have a deterministic method that computes a separating linear form of bit size O(n log n + d + B) in O(n^2 d^2) arithmetic operations of bit-size O(B) in time O(n^2 (log n)^2 d^2 (log B)^2).
our approach is optimal in the worst-case scenario, i.e., the complexity of our algorithms is essentially the best possible complexity.
the complexity of our algorithms is polynomial in n and in the total degree and exponential in the bitsize of input polynomials.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bit complexity of solving a zero-dimensional polynomial systems is essentially the cost of carrying our projections.

we are able to compute a separating hyperplane with small coefficients for a zero-dimensional polynomial ideal in time that depends polynomially on the number of variables and the degree of the polynomials, but only logarithmically on their bitsize.
we have developed a complete and certified method for computing all solutions of zero-dimensional systems with a bit complexity that is essentially linear in the input size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complexity of the considered problems depends on the number of variables but not on the number of polynomials, thus being independent of the dimension of the polynomial system.
, for the problems we consider, projection can be used as a powerful and versatile tool for solving polynomial systems.

, in order to compute a separating linear form, it suffices to carry out projections of the solution set along O(n) directions and that the complexity is essentially determined by the cost of these projections.
